label: The exhibition
heading: Six panels
intro: Each panel holds artworks and the science side by side — never separated. The colour tells you which register you are in: magenta is the science layer, drawn from the fluorescent tag in the Barik Lab micrographs.

panels.title: Somatosensory system
panels.text: The body’s largest sensory apparatus — the whole skin and musculature — reading mechanical, thermal and chemical signals, and holding proprioception, the sense of where the body is in space.

images.caption: Miniscope calcium imaging, mouse thalamus during cold pain — a single frame from the recording · Barik Lab, IISc

panels.title: Pain in the brain
panels.text: Pain is processed and ultimately felt in the brain — and it can be modulated. A person in a coma senses no pain; a soldier fights on injured; hunger can eclipse a wound. In the Barik Lab, the lateral hypothalamus emerges as a hub where emotional states — stress, anxiety — are translated, through the brainstem and spinal cord, into the modulation of pain and itch. A few hundred neurons out of billions, lit up by mouse genetics, are enough.

cards.label: How to read a c-Fos image
cards.title: Ninety minutes late
cards.text:
c-Fos is a protein that active neurons begin to make. It builds up slowly: in most studies it peaks roughly 90 to 120 minutes after the stimulus, though the timing varies with the stimulus and the brain region.

So a c-Fos image is not a live picture of pain. It is an after-image, a trace of what a group of cells did a little while earlier. Khushbu Patel's [Diary Pages](#diary) record time another way, one page at a time, by hand.

panels.title: Opioids / poppy
panels.text: Papaver somniferum runs through Assyrian, Sumerian, Egyptian and Chinese medicine. The body also makes its own opioids, released by hard exertion, and morphine works by borrowing the same receptors. That borrowing has a cost. In the United States, overdose deaths came in three waves: prescription painkillers from the late 1990s, heroin from 2010, and illegally made fentanyl from 2013. Between 1999 and 2023 about 806,000 people there died of an opioid overdose, and in 2017 the crisis was declared a public health emergency. The molecule that eases pain can also end a life.

panels.title: Overcoming
panels.text: In the trenches, in devotion and ritual, brain mechanisms defer pain in favour of something judged more urgent. Expectation does it too. Treating wounded soldiers in the Second World War, the anaesthetist Henry Beecher saw that how much pain people report depends on context as much as on the injury. In 1978, Levine and colleagues showed that placebo pain relief disappears when the opioid blocker naloxone is given: the brain had been releasing its own opioids. And morphine injected in front of a patient relieves more pain than the same dose given out of sight. What we expect is part of the dose.

links.label: How placebo pain relief came to be studied — Benedetti, Frontiers in Pain Research, 2022

panels.title: Anxiety and depression
panels.text: Chronic pain patients often develop both. Relieving the pain often doesn’t relieve the anxiety — the pain- and anxiety-encoding regions interact, and those connections are impaired in chronic pain.

panels.title: Tactile sensation
panels.text: Touch as a social bond — a caress, petting a dog — carried by specialised cutaneous receptors connected to nerves. Touch is not one sense but a landscape of them. Merkel cells read gentle pressure, Meissner corpuscles catch the flutter of something sliding over a fingertip, Ruffini endings register the skin stretching, Pacinian corpuscles feel deep vibration, and fibres wrapped around hair follicles sense a stroke. Sorting nerve cells by the genes they use has so far found about 18 kinds, some tuned to a caress, others to temperature, irritants and painful heat: the same skin carries comfort and alarm.
